endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Governance tools and protocols that are applied to other types of AI systems can be applied to GAI systems. These plans and actions include: • Accessibility and reasonable accommodations

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: This may involve developing user-friendly interfaces and patient-centric applications that allow patients to access their data, view personalized insights, and actively engage in their plans all using easily understandable language to convey their health status and enable them to make more informed decisions regarding their care.

endorsements.title: Achieving health equity through conversational AI: A roadmap for design and implementation of inclusive chatbots in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Ensure the ease of use for those with lower literacy or disability

endorsements.title: Future Perspectives in Radiology: Artificial Intelligence for Responsible Imaging (AIRI)
endorsements.quote: Developing accessibility features for AIRI would include text-to-speech, closed captioning, and easy-to-use interactive interfaces to ensure the AI tool is accessible.

endorsements.title: Advancing neurotech justice in youth digital mental health: insights from an interdisciplinary and cross-generational workshop
endorsements.quote: For instance, integrating customizable settings to accommodate users with disabilities ensures that technology adapts to users rather than forcing users to adapt to the technology.

endorsements.title: Foundation for Artificial Intelligence-Driven Democratization of Healthcare Access
endorsements.quote: The usability imperative further necessitates the development of sophisticated multilingual interface systems that demonstrate substantial adaptability to the various literacy levels and technological proficiencies prevalent within heterogeneous target populations, acknowledging the considerable variation in digital literacy that exists across demographic groups [ 20 ].

endorsements.title: Participatory Digital Twins for Chronic Care: From Predictive Models to Shared Sensemaking
endorsements.quote: Therefore, PDTs should incorporate translation mechanisms, potentially including GenAI-mediated dialogue, that allow users to ask questions, request clarification, and explore alternatives in plain language.

endorsements.title: Multimodal generative AI for pre-practicum mental health support competency development: a human-supervised framework for education-childcare partnerships
endorsements.quote: Accessible interfaces, language support, equivalent non-AI task formats, and reasonable participation alternatives help separate the target competence from digital familiarity.

commentary.bottom_line: Eight sources endorse accessible AI interfaces and reasonable accommodations, but no supplied study tests whether these practices improve use or reduce harm for people with disabilities or diverse needs. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and framework guidance rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard. Six of the eight endorsements are commentaries, and the two frameworks use permissive "may" language. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without comparative data does not support a certainty rating, so the evidence base for this recommendation is empty.

NIST AI 600-1 lists accessibility and reasonable accommodations among governance actions that carry over from other AI systems to generative AI. The CHAI guide frames user-friendly interfaces as something a system may develop. Neither source reports data on whether these measures change access or outcomes for users with disabilities.

Several commentaries name lower literacy, disability, and multilingual needs as design targets for chatbots and patient-facing tools. Because no study was supplied, there is no evidence on whether accessible designs reach Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients or improve their experience.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study compares accessible or accommodated AI interfaces with standard interfaces on task completion, comprehension, errors, or harm among patients with disabilities, limited literacy, or limited English proficiency. No study documents how often current AI tools exclude or harm these users. Evaluations that measure both the size of the hazard and the effect of specific features such as text-to-speech, captioning, plain-language output, and non-AI alternatives would give health systems a basis for setting priorities.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The endorsements name these groups as intended beneficiaries, but whether accessible AI interfaces serve them remains unmeasured.
